summary: A TCP connection is closed independently in each direction using FIN segments, so a full close normally takes four segments. The side that closes first lingers in TIME-WAIT to make sure the final ACK arrives and old segments die out.

sections.heading: Normal close (RFC 9293, section 3.6)
sections.code:
Active closer                    Passive closer
ESTABLISHED                      ESTABLISHED
  --- FIN seq=x ------------->
FIN-WAIT-1                       CLOSE-WAIT
  <-- ACK ack=x+1 -----------
FIN-WAIT-2
                                 (app calls close)
  <-- FIN seq=y ------------
                                 LAST-ACK
  --- ACK ack=y+1 ---------->
TIME-WAIT (2 x MSL)              CLOSED
CLOSED

sections.heading: State meanings
bullets: FIN-WAIT-1: our FIN sent, waiting for its ACK.
FIN-WAIT-2: our FIN acknowledged, waiting for the peer's FIN.
CLOSE-WAIT: peer's FIN received; waiting for our application to close.
LAST-ACK: our FIN sent after CLOSE-WAIT; waiting for the final ACK.
TIME-WAIT: waiting before deleting the connection record.
CLOSING: both sides sent FIN simultaneously.

sections.heading: Why four segments
sections.body: Each direction is closed separately. The peer may still have data to send after receiving our FIN (a half-close), so its ACK and its own FIN can be separated in time. If it has nothing more to send they can be combined, giving three segments.

sections.heading: TIME-WAIT
sections.body: The active closer must remain in TIME-WAIT for 2 x MSL (RFC 9293 requires 2 x the maximum segment lifetime; MSL is commonly assumed 60 s on Linux, giving a 60 s wait in practice). It guarantees the last ACK can be retransmitted if lost and prevents delayed segments from a previous connection being mistaken for a new one using the same 4-tuple.

sections.heading: Abortive close
sections.body: A RST ends a connection immediately with no handshake. It is sent for segments to a non-existent connection and when SO_LINGER with zero timeout is used. Pending data is discarded.
An application can send a FIN yet keep reading, as in HTTP clients that signal 'request done' while waiting for the response. shutdown(fd, SHUT_WR) does this; close() ends both directions.

Servers that actively close thousands of connections per second accumulate TIME-WAIT entries and may exhaust ephemeral ports. Remedies: let the client close first, reuse connections (keep-alive), and use SO_REUSEADDR or tcp_tw_reuse for outgoing connections.
CLOSE-WAIT piling up means the peer closed but the local application never called close(), a classic file-descriptor leak. TIME-WAIT is normal; CLOSE-WAIT growth is not.
Both go FIN-WAIT-1 -> CLOSING -> TIME-WAIT after exchanging FINs and ACKs; each side waits 2 x MSL.
`ss -tan state time-wait | wc -l` counts TIME-WAIT sockets; `ss -tan` lists all TCP states.

takeaways: Each direction closes with its own FIN and ACK, usually four segments.
The active closer ends in TIME-WAIT for 2 x MSL.
CLOSE-WAIT buildup indicates an application not closing sockets.

references.label: RFC 1337: TIME-WAIT Assassination Hazards in TCP
